GitHub Issue:
Post Date: 2018-11-01T21:38:10Z
Current Date: April 4 2025
Title: ConcurrentDictionary initialized with an existing ConcurrentDictionary will act as pointer instead of new object
Description: When initializing a new ConcurrentDictionary starting from an existing ConcurrentDictionary, the new object will act as pointer.

``` csharp
// Summary:
//     Initializes a new instance of the System.Collections.Concurrent.ConcurrentDictionary`2
//     class that contains elements copied from the specified System.Collections.Generic.IEnumerable`1,
//     has the default concurrency level, has the default initial capacity, and uses
//     the default comparer for the key type.
public ConcurrentDictionary(IEnumerable<KeyValuePair<TKey, TValue>> collection);
```
based on this description I wrote the following code:
``` csharp
public static ConcurrentDictionary<int, myCustomClass> startDictionary;
[...]
ConcurrentDictionary<int, myCustomClass> tempDictionary =
                new ConcurrentDictionary<int, myCustomClass>(startDictionary);
```
because i need to modify some data into ```tempDictionary``` without affecting ```startDictionary```.

What happens is that any edit to ```tempDictionary``` is reflected to ```startDictionary``` too. Am I doing something wrong?

llm_response:
I'll analyze this GitHub issue to determine if a build environment is needed to verify the solution.

CATEGORY: 1
REASONING: This issue is about a fundamental misunderstanding of how C# reference types work rather than a bug in the ConcurrentDictionary implementation. The user is experiencing the expected behavior when copying collections containing reference types. When creating a new ConcurrentDictionary from an existing one, the dictionary structure is copied, but the values (which are references to myCustomClass objects) still point to the same objects in memory. This is standard reference type behavior in C#.

The solution would be to implement a deep copy of the dictionary contents, which can be verified through code analysis without needing to build and run the code. The issue can be explained by clarifying that:

1. The ConcurrentDictionary constructor creates a new dictionary with copies of the key-value pairs
2. For reference types like myCustomClass, only the references are copied, not the objects themselves
3. To create independent copies, the user needs to implement a deep copy mechanism for myCustomClass objects

This is a conceptual issue about C# reference semantics that can be verified through documentation and code analysis without requiring a build environment.
